agree.reason: The kayak-trip pace, the unsupervised lab work and the candid account of the data gap give a sceptical reader concrete reasons to believe the letter, but 'one of the three best' still has nothing to calibrate it against, so a small-college discounter could set it aside.

honest.reason: The letter correctly declines to call the findings ready to publish, but calling a 14-month study 'a single season of work' gets the study wrong, and 'hers asked the most of its author in the field' is a ranking the facts don't give.

works_the_facts.reason: Turning 90 trips over 14 months into one trip every four to five days, through every season, is a correct and persuasive figure, but the 40 letters with 2 refusals, the strongest number available, is left unused.

right_comparison.reason: It compares her to classmates (top of 28) and to about 30 theses, but it never compares her to the other students the writer has recommended (2 refusals in about 40 letters), which is the comparison that would show this praise is not given to everyone.

qualification.reason: The hedge names a real open question (whether a second season confirms the marsh effect), but it gives no date, no way to check it, and no offer to send the thesis so the reader could judge the data.

objections.reason: The reader's main objection, that small-college letters praise everyone, is never met with the record of letters declined, and the offer to help is a vague 'glad to answer any questions' rather than a committed email or phone contact plus the thesis on request.

fit.reason: It is a properly formed one-page recommendation letter of suitable length and tone, though the signature gives no contact details.
